lyrics:
Today’s assignment
Write a letter
To the man who keeps us safe
Use your finest handwriting
Include the date
Remember gratitude
Dear Leader
My name is Anna
I am twelve years old today
I attend Continuance School
In Residential Zone Eight
My teacher says you read our letters
He says every child is heard
So I checked my spelling twice
And used my very neatest words
Thank you for the quiet streets
And doors that lock at half past six
Thank you for the hallway cameras
They report when something slips
Thank you for the Red Shirt crossing guard
He knows each student’s face
He asks where Mother plans to go
So no one gets misplaced
One clear voice
One clear rule
One safe road
From home to school
One true screen
One daily word
Nothing false
Is ever heard
Dear Leader, I am happy
Everything is where it goes
Dear Leader, I am happy
Someone watches, someone knows
Every morning has instructions
Every question has a key
Dear Leader, I am happy
Thank you for remembering me
Grandma says there used to be
A dozen channels after supper
People argued over facts
And children heard opposing answers
That sounds noisy
That sounds lonely
How could anyone decide
Now the evening news is simple
And the borders stay outside
We used to have more countries
On the classroom map, they say
But our new one is much cleaner
All the colors match today
One clear voice
One clear rule
One safe road
From home to school
One true screen
One daily word
Nothing false
Is ever heard
Dear Leader, I am happy
Everything is where it goes
Dear Leader, I am happy
Someone watches, someone knows
Every morning has instructions
Every question has a key
Dear Leader, I am happy
Thank you for remembering me

Very good
Again from measure five
Greatest country
That Ever lived
Safe and clean
And fully paid
My father works at Forecast Center
He corrects events before they start
My mother says the system helps him
Keep bad choices far apart
Our neighbor moved last Tuesday
Teacher says he found new work
His windows have been painted white
His dog still waits beside the curb
I gave the dog my lunch on Friday
The crossing guard recorded that
He said compassion is permitted
When entered in the proper app
When I grow up, I want to help
Arrange the things people believe
I want to work inside the system
That decides what they receive
I will never leave Outlandia
There is nowhere else I need

Every book has been agreed

Excellent, Anna

persona:
Michael Anthony Rose is a songwriter of rare insight and startling honesty. On his debut for Maricopa Records, he uses direct, unadorned language to explore the most profound human experiences: the gulf between who we were and who we are, the search for truth in a world of convenient fictions, and the quiet defiance of living an authentic life. His songs are less stories than they are confessions, built from the concrete details of a lived experience, where a reflection in a phone screen or the memory of a dream can trigger a lifetime of contemplation. Rose doesn't just sing about life; he holds a mirror up to it, capturing the small, resonant moments of realization that define us.

The central preoccupations of Rose's work are time and memory. His lyrics trace the lines from lost childhood potential to the stark realities of aging, questioning what we build to outlast ourselves and what we must learn to let go. He writes with a philosopher's curiosity and a diarist's intimacy, exploring the comfort of a shared lie in one song and the freedom of embracing dissonance in the next. This is music that navigates regret, loss, and mortality with a steady, empathetic gaze, always returning to the challenge of being present for the life one actually has, not the one that was planned.

Throughout his work, Rose reveals a vast emotional landscape. His voice moves from the raw vulnerability of admitting fear and bitterness to the quiet strength of asserting one’s own space and worth. He sings of intimate connection with a sensory richness and of profound disconnection with a heartbreaking clarity. His perspective is that of a seasoned witness, one who sees the innocence in younger generations without envy and accepts the limitations of his own body without surrender. He finds resilience not by ignoring the damage, but by standing within it and refusing to be diminished.

In the songs of Michael Anthony Rose, listeners will not find easy answers or false comfort. Instead, they will find a voice that speaks with clarity and courage to the complexities of a full-size life. It is an invitation to stop arguing with the truth, to witness the ordinary light of the day, and to find that being here, honestly and without shame, is more than enough.

impression.text: The track presents a bright, uncanny cheerfulness, blending bubbly synth-pop textures with a pristine children's choir to create an eerie, dystopian musical theatre atmosphere. The energy is consistently high and bouncy, driven by a crisp, syncopated rhythm section and playful melodic lines that feel unsettlingly wholesome. The production is exceptionally polished and spacious, featuring a clean mix where the upfront lead vocals sit perfectly amidst lush harmonies, acoustic guitar, and sparkling synthesizer elements. A distinctive moment occurs near the end with the intrusion of a commanding adult male voice, emphasizing the song's conceptual narrative before it concludes with a cheerful instrumental outro.

review.review_text: The genius of "Dear Leader" is that it never winks at you. Anna is twelve, she checks her spelling twice, and she means every word: that sincerity, delivered in a bright child's voice over upright piano, glockenspiel and pizzicato strings at a gentle 89 BPM in G major, is exactly what makes the skin crawl. Rose builds the whole thing as a school recital, and the arrangement plays it straight, the recorders and classroom harmonies leaning warmer and prettier just as the lyrics turn most chilling: "His windows have been painted white / His dog still waits beside the curb." The pre-chorus works like a catechism, "One clear voice / One clear rule," and the hook lands its awful comfort on "Someone watches, someone knows." What keeps this from being a mere concept-piece stunt is the restraint. Where a lesser writer would reach for menace or a horror-choir cliche, Rose lets the fanfare interlude and the teacher's clipped "Again from measure five" carry the dread by implication. The closing contralto coda, flat and retrospective, is the masterstroke: "She was not hiding any message. / She believed each word she wrote." It denies you the relief of irony. At nearly five minutes the middle verse runs a touch long before the bridge reclaims the tension, but that is a small thing against how completely the trick works. This is Randy Newman's cruel civility crossed with a grade-school pageant, and it earns its place at the front of the record.
